title: Aggregation size and overwintering survival in ectoparasitic swallow bugs Cimex vicarius (Hemiptera: Cimicidae)
content:
Abstract
One potential benefit of aggregating in various animals is a reduction in water loss, lowered respiration rates, and (for endotherms) enhanced heat conservation, especially in stressful times such as overwintering. The physiological advantages of aggregating are often assumed to increase with aggregation size, but relatively little information is available to know whether these advantages translate to fitness metrics such as overwintering survival. We examined the natural distribution of aggregation sizes in the overwintering swallow bug (Cimex vicarius), an ectoparasite of the colonially nesting cliff swallow (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota). In western Nebraska, overwintering aggregations varied from 1 to ∼2000 swallow bugs per nest; aggregation sizes were larger later in the summer and at sites that had earlier hosted larger cliff swallow colonies. Field-collected bugs were housed in environmental chambers in groups of 5, 10, 50, 100, 250, and 500 bugs, and survival was measured from August to late April. An elevation of 3 °C, relative to natural wintertime temperatures, allowed us to assess the potential effects of global warming on the overwintering survival of different group sizes. For swallow bugs held at temperatures to which they would have been exposed in the field, overwintering survival was highest for individuals in the smallest group (5 bugs), and survival was significantly lowest for the largest group (500 bugs). The group-size effect disappeared under the elevated temperature regime, with no significant differences among aggregation sizes. The results indicate that swallow bugs likely derive no physiological benefits from aggregating, and grouping in winter may be costly to fitness.
